title: P. R. Gibson, the boss Memphis pianist
summary: Slim corrects the name to P. R. Gibson and praises his schooling, style and playing for the Union.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Uh, you mentioned, uh, Piano Gibson to Paul Oliver. Could you tell me more about that? Oh, you mean Piano Gibson? Uh, Piano Gibson, Loomis Gibson, he played on Beatles Street and Memphis.

Oh, no, they got the wrong name. His name is P. R. Gibson. And, brother, do you know P. R. Gibson? Yes. That's a bad man. His mother graduated him, uh, at, he went to school and, uh, he wasn't, because people didn't get the education.

He's a boss piano player. Respected by Orlheim, Duke, and anybody. Is he still living? I saw... I think he is, but he, he, uh, he's the man reminding me how to, uh, stretch my fingers. Always, I had that old trap style, you know, and, uh, I was, uh, always wanted to be a tent man, you know, like, in old timers, that, uh, as Miss Slim, his old partner, Rabbit, you know, the tent, and them walk in them tents, and, and that was for the shuffle like Louis J. come out back in them days. So, P. R. was graduated. He, anything called at the, at the, at, at, uh, 214th Bieland, the Union, they called for P. R. It's traded out. He was a boss, a scholar. And he, he didn't, he just could play. Fats, uh, pounds, everything he played, and, uh, he played on style. But he never made no records, not designed, no, unless he made some lately. But he played with Roosevelt Sax, after when Roosevelt Sax left here, and, uh, some years, after he quit driving care, of course, Roosevelt, he really just didn't have a touch, because, see, like a brother at Piara, they plays a, a outstanding playing piano. A real outstanding, is what I mean. I don't say fangling, you know, a lot of legitimate stuff, you know, executing like a leech, but some brother plays a clean piano, just like the old time church songs in my book. Uh huh. They tell the story, with the other words, I come down to a song, I say that tells the story. My Haley Jackson move went up a little high. And when, if I could hear my mother pray. And when the trumpet sounded. The people were singing, soul singing then, you understand what I mean? Yes. It wasn't too much jazzy stuff, you know, it was a, it was a religious feeling.
